components.text: Challenges the premise that being caused entails being necessitated or predetermined by prior events.
Does not yet explain how non-necessitated causation supplies control rather than indeterminacy.
The skeptical dilemma allegedly conflates being caused with being necessitated by prior events.
A complete answer must explain positively how non-necessitating causation supplies control rather than randomness.
Offers introspective observation of choosing mental activation as evidence for controlled agency.
Does not explain why the observed choice escapes both determination and indeterminacy.
The relevant capacity is allegedly observable in choosing whether to activate rational attention.
The observation must distinguish controlled agency from a determined or indeterminate appearance of control.
Reframes the motion-relevant freedom as activating rational engagement rather than ultimate authorship of every outcome.
Preserves the control issue by locating it in whether the rational faculty is voluntarily activated.
The proper issue is limited voluntary activation of reason rather than authorship of every action or content.
The narrower capacity must still survive the skeptic's determination-or-randomness challenge.
Answers the dilemma by positing the agent as the cause of a choice that is neither causeless nor prior-event necessitated.
Does not provide a mechanism or criterion distinguishing agent causation from unexplained indeterminacy.
A choice can be caused by the agent without being causeless or necessitated by prior factors.
The account must explain how agent causation differs from an unexplained label for indeterminacy.
Identifies the inference from felt immediacy to the truth of its causal interpretation as invalid.
Does not independently resolve whether agent causation is coherent.
Feeling or observing an apparent force or agency does not establish the truth of its interpretation.
The reply does not independently show that the experienced agency is determined or random.
Examines the city exercise and argues that candidate thoughts arise without proactive selection.
Does not fully address the narrower claim that method or degree of attention, rather than content, is chosen.
Observed deliberation contains thoughts and options that arise without proactive selection by a chooser.
Unchosen content does not by itself refute voluntary selection of the method or degree of attention.
Challenges agent authorship by tracing conscious action to desires whose existence and operative strength are unchosen.
Does not exclude the possibility that chosen rational engagement alters which desire becomes operative.
Conscious conduct allegedly follows operative desires whose existence and relative strength were not freely chosen.
The account must explain whether rational attention can revise or reorder desires over time.
Explains that unbidden subconscious content does not answer the distinct claim that conscious method is chosen.
Claims chosen method can affect the governing desire but does not fully explain that causal influence.
The skeptical example concerns unchosen content, while the defended freedom concerns the chosen method of engagement.
Chosen rational method can affect which desire governs action, but the causal independence of that method remains unexplained.
Applies the caused-or-causeless dilemma directly to the alleged agent-caused mental event.
Treats caused events as falling under determining causes without fully answering the cause-versus-necessitation distinction.
Extends the dilemma to mental method choice but does not separately analyze attentional regulation.
Calling the agent a cause does not explain control if the mental event remains caused or causeless.
The reply treats caused events as determined without fully defending why causation entails necessitation.
The same dilemma is applied to mental method, though the selected excerpt does not develop that application fully.
Asserts a nonphysical mind but does not show why its choices escape the caused-or-causeless dilemma.
Provides contrary metaphysical material without answering the dilemma's theory-independent structure.
The causal dilemma applies to mental events regardless of whether mind reduces to matter.
The move asserts nonphysical consciousness and choice but does not explain a third control-conferring causal relation.
Answers the fixed-desire picture by arguing that repeated reasoning revises value judgments and later emotions.
Does not establish that the earlier choices to reason were themselves freely selected.
Does not resolve the causal status of the self-shaping choices.
Repeated rational choices can revise value judgments and thereby alter later emotions and operative desires.
The response does not show that the repeated choices themselves escape determining causes or indeterminacy.
Argues that a person can evade recognized considerations rather than being compelled by rational content.
Reasserts direct introspective evidence without answering why its causal interpretation might be mistaken.
Does not explain whether evasion is determined, agent-caused, or indeterminate.
Observable evasion allegedly demonstrates that recognized evidence does not mechanically compel rational acceptance.
The move does not answer the objection that introspection may misidentify the causal source of evasion.
It shows apparent resistance to content but not proactive selection of the content that arises.
Reiterates that introspection alone cannot establish free will when a philosophical defeater is available.
Preserves ordinary experiential trust while denying that it resolves the special causal question.
Does not depend on rejecting the defender's account of consciousness.
Introspection alone cannot establish free will when philosophical arguments support alternative causal explanations.
Ordinary trust in experience is preserved while the stronger metaphysical inference is treated as defeasible.
States that the anti-free-will argument does not depend on materialism and therefore survives a nonphysical mind.
Does not independently demonstrate that agent causation is incoherent under every theory of consciousness.
Does not separately analyze whether a theory-neutral focus capacity is coherent.
Rejecting materialism does not answer a causal objection designed to apply across theories of consciousness.
The passage asserts theory independence but only compresses the underlying reason agent causation remains incoherent.
Reframes coercion as limiting the exercise and available outputs of a capacity rather than eliminating the capacity itself.
Does not answer the general causal incoherence argument.
Does not establish that the remaining judgment under coercion escapes desire governance.
External force can restrict the exercise of rational choice without eliminating the underlying faculty.
The response does not establish that constrained selection is independent of operative desires.
Specifies the relevant alternatives as degrees and methods of mental activation rather than arbitrary content selection.
Directly preserves unbidden content while locating the claimed choice in full-context engagement, drift, or evasion.
Does not explain how graded activation escapes the theory-independent causal dilemma.
The relevant freedom concerns degrees and methods of mental activation, not unrestricted selection of content or outcome.
The scope clarification does not explain how graded activation escapes the causal dilemma.
It expressly concedes unchosen content while relocating freedom to engagement method.
Agrees that coercion restricts meaningful options while maintaining that conscious surrender remains technically a choice.
Does not determine whether the conscious selection or its degree of engagement is freely authored.
Coercion can leave a conscious selection between alternatives even when ordinary speech calls the conduct forced.
The reply does not show whether conscious selection includes freely controlled mental activation.
